segments.title: A Royal Navy answer to Japan's Number 13 class
segments.body: The Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts challenge puts a 33-knot British answer to Japan's Number 13 design inside a 58,000-ton full-load limit. Drachinifel abandons the battleship hull when the game's machinery weight leaves almost no allowance for weapons and armor, then uses a G3-derived battlecruiser hull capped at 55,500 tons. His design carries the required twelve 18-inch guns, an inclined 14.8-inch belt, a 5-inch deck, and 16-inch turret and barbette armor. Alex Clarke retains an N3-style arrangement with nine main guns and a heavier 17-inch belt, which fails the challenge's gun-count requirement. His turret plates are still only 10.6 inches thick when time expires, and the intended addition of turret armor would also help correct excess weight aft. The nine-gun alternative therefore still requires work on both turret protection and balance.

evidence.note: The British design brief sets displacement, speed, main-armament, and protection requirements.
Machinery weight in the game forces a switch from a battleship hull to the G3 battlecruiser hull.
The battlecruiser hull limits the design to 55,500 tons.
The completed designs differ in gun count, belt and turret protection, and unfinished weight distribution.

segments.summary: A simulated British response to Japan's Number 13 design tests whether twelve 18-inch guns, 33 knots, and heavy protection can fit within 58,000 tons.

segments.title: Could a dreadnought carry Aegis and VLS?
segments.body: A dreadnought hull could accommodate modern weapons after sufficiently extensive reconstruction, but the practical case depends on which hull is available and how much of it is retained. Main-gun blast and shock threaten delicate electronics, while Aegis radar and computers require substantial electrical generation. Existing barbettes also complicate the placement of vertical-launch cells. USS Mississippi's postwar missile-test role provides an example of adapting a battleship for guided weapons, and Aegis proposals for the Iowa-class ships, Newport News, and Salem demonstrate the wider interest in such conversions. A refit on this scale needs dry docks, cranes, and supporting shipyard facilities. A navy with that industrial capacity can also build a new hull, which weakens the argument for an extreme reconstruction.

evidence.note: Aegis and missile conversion raise problems of gun shock, electrical generation, existing barbettes, and shipyard capacity, with earlier battleship and cruiser proposals as comparisons.

segments.summary: Fitting modern sensors and missiles into an old battleship is technically possible, but gun shock, electrical demand, and the scale of reconstruction undermine its practicality.
segments.question: How far could a dreadnought hull be upgraded with Aegis, helicopter facilities, and VLS?
segments.answerShort: Extensive reconstruction could make it possible, but gun blast, power demand, internal obstructions, and shipyard requirements make the practical case doubtful.

segments.title: Where to put extra generators during a dreadnought refit
segments.body: Adding a generating shed on deck appears easier than reaching machinery spaces beneath an old dreadnought's existing structure. That location introduces noise and exposes another installation to gun blast and heat. The generator itself also need not occupy an enormous compartment: its rotor and stator are compared in size with a Ford Fiesta. A dreadnought can contain that volume, particularly if the refit removes barbettes. Choosing where to install the machinery therefore involves protection and access as well as finding enough space.

evidence.note: A proposal to add a generator on deck prompts concerns about noise, blast, and heat, followed by a comparison of generator size with available internal volume.

segments.summary: A generator on deck avoids difficult access below, but noise, blast, and heat complicate that apparently simple refit option.

segments.title: Why empty VLS weight does not determine a battleship conversion
segments.body: Removing main turrets creates substantial room for vertical-launch cells, but the amount of reconstruction still determines what can fit. The existing internal arrangement could prevent a converted dreadnought from carrying as many missiles as its overall size suggests. An arsenal ship starts with missile capacity as its principal design purpose, while an Arleigh Burke or Ticonderoga could use its space more efficiently than an adapted battleship. Stability is raised as a question, without a definitive calculation. A quoted open-source estimate gives about 15 tons for eight strike-length Mark 41 cells, explicitly excluding the missiles. That figure describes the launcher structure and does not settle the complete conversion's weight or arrangement.

evidence.note: The extent of reconstruction, existing internal arrangement, possible stability issues, and comparisons with arsenal ships and modern missile warships qualify the available VLS capacity.
The quoted estimate is about 15 tons for eight strike-length Mark 41 cells without missiles.

segments.summary: Turret removal creates space for missiles, but internal layout and the difference between empty launchers and a complete installation still matter.

segments.title: An antiaircraft secondary battery for the Number 13 response
segments.body: Drachinifel's simulated British design carries four twin 4-inch mounts along each side amidships and two more twin mounts aft on the centerline. That arrangement provides twelve 4-inch guns on a broadside for antiaircraft fire. Quadruple 2-inch mounts represent pom-poms in the game, with their concentration behind the bridge inspired by the initial King George V arrangement. This produces an unusually heavy antiaircraft fit for the early 1930s, while omitting torpedo armament. Protection uses a 14.8-inch belt and 5-inch deck in an all-or-nothing scheme, with weight saved on the conning tower while retaining 16-inch turret and barbette armor.

evidence.note: The 4-inch mounting layout, game equivalents for pom-poms, absence of torpedoes, and contrasting protection of the conning tower and main armament define the design.

segments.summary: Ten twin 4-inch mounts and simulated pom-poms give the British design a heavy antiaircraft fit while armor weight favors the main armament over the conning tower.

segments.title: Italy's 1929 answer to the Nelson class
segments.body: The simulated Regia Marina brief uses a 1929 early-construction allowance to seek a 35,000-ton battleship with 381 mm guns, 30 knots, and enough range for Mediterranean operations. Drachinifel produces a treaty-scale forerunner of the Littorio arrangement with triple 15-inch turrets, a 14-inch belt, an elevated triple 6-inch secondary mount, and exposed deck torpedoes. The unusually high secondary turret results from the game's limited barbette choices, which provide either too little clearance or excessive height. Alex Clarke instead fits twelve 15-inch/50 guns, eighteen 6-inch guns, 30-knot machinery, and a 14.4-inch belt into a design below the stated displacement ceiling. He can increase the displayed range to 11,000 km while bringing the displacement to about 34,000 tons. The twelve-gun design wins on firepower, but its single fire-control center and obstructed bridge view remain serious weaknesses.

evidence.note: The Italian brief specifies the early-construction allowance, 35,000-ton limit, 381 mm guns, 30 knots, Mediterranean range, and preferred triple turrets.
Drachinifel's design is compared with a treaty-compliant Littorio-style ship.
The competing designs differ in main armament and protection, while limited barbette options, exposed torpedoes, range settings, and fire-control arrangements introduce further compromises.

segments.summary: A simulated Italian answer to Nelson combines 381 mm guns and 30 knots within 35,000 tons, then exposes compromises in secondary mounting and fire control.

segments.title: Would gun blast endanger deck-mounted torpedoes?
segments.body: The Italian design's torpedo launchers sit exposed on deck near the main battery's firing arcs. No measured shock-tolerance figure is supplied for the contemporary torpedoes. Drachinifel intends to expend them early: they could be fired in a close Mediterranean engagement or used as spoiling shots to disrupt an opponent's maneuvering at longer range. Keeping them aboard through a prolonged gunfight would leave them exposed while the main guns repeatedly fired overhead. The proposed tactic therefore limits how long the ship carries this vulnerable armament during an action.

evidence.note: Early torpedo launches in a close action or as spoiling shots would avoid retaining exposed weapons through prolonged main-gun fire.

segments.summary: The exposed deck torpedoes would be fired early, either at close range or as spoiling shots before a prolonged gun duel.
segments.question: How sensitive would torpedoes of this era be to the concussive shock of the battleship's own guns?
segments.answerShort: Their shock tolerance is not quantified. The proposed response is to fire the exposed torpedoes early, before repeated main-gun fire over the launchers.

segments.title: Twelve main guns with only one fire-control center
segments.body: The twelve-gun Italian design has only one fire-control center. A disabling hit there would leave the turrets relying on their own aiming arrangements. HMS Rodney is invoked as the imagined opponent capable of destroying that forward position. The view from the bridge is also obstructed in the game model. These weaknesses qualify the earlier judgment that superior main-battery firepower makes this the winning design.

evidence.note: The verdict favors the twelve-gun battery, followed by objections to a single fire-control center and obstructed bridge view.

segments.summary: The Italian design's heavy battery depends on one vulnerable fire-control center, while its bridge also has an obstructed view.

segments.title: An 80,000-ton American Pacific battleship
segments.body: The 1940 game exercise allows an American fast battleship of up to 80,000 tons at full load, with at least 28 knots and guns of 16 inches or larger. The ship is treated as an alternative to Montana, with an 8,000-nautical-mile requirement for reaching the Philippines from the US west coast and permission to use the intended expanded Panama Canal locks. Drachinifel fits twenty 16-inch/50 guns, a 16-inch belt, a 6-inch deck, and 28-knot machinery into just over 79,000 tons, with a stated range of 26,000 kilometers. Clarke chooses twelve 18-inch/50 guns, a 17-inch belt, and 29 knots. Secondary armament also remains open to historical alternatives: experimental twin dual-purpose 6-inch weapons are mentioned as an option considered in some Montana designs. Even this displacement allowance leaves decisions about protection, machinery, and the space available for secondary weapons.

evidence.note: The 1940 brief sets an 80,000-ton full-load ceiling, at least 28 knots, guns of 16 inches or larger, and a Pacific role as an alternative to Montana.
The 8,000-nautical-mile requirement, experimental twin dual-purpose 6-inch option, and intended expanded Panama Canal locks.
The twenty-gun and twelve-gun designs, including their speed, protection, range, and different approaches to main-battery firepower.

segments.summary: Two 1940 game designs use an 80,000-ton allowance for either twenty 16-inch guns or twelve 18-inch guns, with Pacific range and enlarged canal locks shaping the hull.

segments.title: Could an 80,000-ton battleship exceed Panamax?
segments.body: The American design exercise permits the additional beam associated with the intended expanded Panama Canal locks. Those locks are linked to plans for accommodating the Montana class. The proposed battleship can therefore be wider than Iowa instead of squeezing 80,000 tons into the existing Panamax limits. Its permissible dimensions depend on the shore infrastructure assumed in the scenario.

evidence.note: Permission to use the intended expanded locks associated with Montana planning, allowing greater beam than Iowa.

segments.summary: The assumed expansion of the Panama Canal locks permits a beam wider than Iowa's for the 80,000-ton American design.
segments.question: Must the proposed 80,000-ton American fast battleship adhere to Panamax dimensions?
segments.answerShort: No; the exercise assumes the intended expanded locks associated with Montana planning, allowing a beam wider than Iowa's.

segments.title: How ammunition reached an 8-inch turret stacked on a 12-inch turret
segments.body: The arrangement places an 8-inch turret directly above a 12-inch mount. Two extra ammunition hoists are recalled as passing through the lower turret to supply the upper guns. This compact layout sought a useful heavy secondary battery within the cost and size limits of the hull. Separate positions for the 8-inch guns would have required a larger ship. The arrangement is judged unsuccessful despite the appeal of concentrating firepower in a small space.

evidence.note: An 8-inch turret above a 12-inch mount, with two ammunition hoists through the lower turret recalled from memory.
Budget and hull-size constraints behind the compact arrangement, which is judged unsuccessful.

segments.summary: The recalled ammunition arrangement feeds a superposed 8-inch turret through two additional hoists inside the lower 12-inch mount.
segments.question: How did an early American battleship feed an 8-inch turret mounted directly above a 12-inch turret?
segments.answerShort: Two additional ammunition hoists are recalled as passing through the lower 12-inch mount to supply the upper 8-inch turret.

segments.title: A British rival for the Kongo contract
segments.body: The game exercise imagines an Armstrong Whitworth counter-offer to Vickers for Japan's Kongo contract, using 1913 British technology and a displacement allowance of about 27,500 tons. Japan's desire for ships individually superior to likely opponents makes extra main guns attractive. Drachinifel offers ten 14-inch guns, a 10-inch belt, and 28 knots, with two more guns than the eight-gun battlecruisers used for comparison. Clarke fits twelve 14-inch guns and 28-knot machinery by using a slimmer hull with greater draft and sharply reducing the secondary battery. His design carries ten 3-inch casemate guns, four torpedo tubes, and a stated range of 19,000 kilometers. The very light secondary armament draws criticism even as the heavier main battery earns the decision. Concentrating firepower in the main battery requires sacrifices elsewhere in the design.

evidence.note: The British counter-offer uses 1913 technology and a displacement limit of about 27,500 tons.
Armstrong Whitworth as the hypothetical rival and Japan's preference for ships individually superior to likely opponents.
The ten-gun and twelve-gun proposals, belt protection, 28-knot speed, light secondary battery, torpedo tubes, range, and hull proportions.

segments.summary: A hypothetical British competitor for Japan's Kongo contract compares a ten-gun battlecruiser with a twelve-gun alternative carrying very light secondaries.

segments.title: Judging South Dakota's electrical system by 1940s practice
segments.body: South Dakota's electrical failures often dominate recollections of the class, leaving its armor and firepower out of the picture. A proposed study would reconstruct the choices that produced its electrical distribution system. Wartime designers lacked today's electronic and digital load balancing, rerouting, and automatic reset systems. Their decisions therefore need to be assessed against contemporary engineering practice. The intended investigation would explain how the system developed before judging it through the failure for which the ship became known.

evidence.note: A proposed study of South Dakota-class electrical design, the prominence of its failure reputation, and the absence of modern automatic distribution controls.

segments.summary: South Dakota's electrical distribution deserves examination against contemporary engineering practice and the control systems available in the 1940s.

segments.title: Why do Massachusetts switchboards show both 440 and 450 volts?
segments.body: Drachinifel recalls a photograph of USS Massachusetts with circuits marked 440 volts and 450 volts on the same breaker equipment. The labels challenge a categorical claim that the ship used 440 volts everywhere. The reason for the difference remains unresolved. Possible explanations include the location of the neutral tap in a transformer or alternator, an incorrectly tapped winding, or a deliberate requirement for a slightly higher-voltage circuit. Experience with mistapped modern transformers supplies an analogy, rather than proof of a fault aboard Massachusetts. The 10-volt difference is also judged small relative to a system operating above 400 volts.

evidence.note: Drachinifel's recollection of Massachusetts breaker equipment labeled with both 440-volt and 450-volt circuits.
Unconfirmed explanations involving neutral taps, winding errors, or a deliberately higher-voltage circuit, with a modern transformer analogy.

segments.summary: Mixed voltage labels prompt several possible explanations, with no confirmed cause for the difference.
segments.question: Why would circuits on the same South Dakota-class switchboard be labeled 440 volts and 450 volts?
segments.answerShort: The cause is unresolved. Suggested explanations involve transformer or alternator taps, a winding error, or a deliberate requirement for a higher-voltage circuit.

segments.title: HMS Belfast's clutch and its 200 rpm operating warning
segments.body: Drachinifel recalls a photograph of HMS Belfast's engine room showing a control labeled as a clutch. Its accompanying notice warns against engaging or disengaging the clutch above 200 rpm. The photograph was offered against a claim that warships with geared turbines did not have clutches. Belfast's equipment provides a specific counterexample, and the operating notice adds a limit on how that equipment should be used.

evidence.note: Drachinifel's recollection of Belfast's clutch control and a notice prohibiting engagement or disengagement above 200 rpm.

segments.summary: A recalled machinery photograph places a clutch aboard a geared-turbine warship and records its operating-speed restriction.

segments.title: German and British 90,000-ton fast battleships
segments.body: The 1944 game exercise pairs a German fast battleship with a British opponent under the same 90,000-ton allowance. Hull structure alone consumes a substantial part of that displacement before weapons and protection are added. Both designs end up with sixteen 16.5-inch guns. The German proposal combines a 20-inch belt with a turtleback protection scheme, while the British Armageddon uses all-or-nothing protection and a thicker deck. The British design also claims a faster rate of fire and a small range advantage. The assessment favors the German ship in a close-range engagement and the British ship at longer ranges, with the first critical hit potentially deciding the fight. The judges split the result because either design could win under the right engagement conditions.

evidence.note: The 1944 German-versus-British brief and the substantial structural weight of a 90,000-ton hull.
The sixteen-gun batteries, German turtleback, British all-or-nothing protection, deck comparison, and claimed rate-of-fire and range advantages.
Close-range and long-range advantages, critical-system damage, and the decision to split the result.

segments.summary: Two hypothetical 90,000-ton battleships converge on sixteen 16.5-inch guns but favor different protection schemes and engagement ranges.

segments.title: Tracks, ramps, and a German midget submarine
segments.body: The small German submarine combined torpedoes with a tracked undercarriage and is remembered as prone to falling over. The suggested explanation for the tracks is that the craft could use launch ramps, reach warehouses for maintenance, and move over land between canals or channels. That purpose is recalled with uncertainty. A simpler alternative proposed is a wheeled carriage onto which the submarine could float before being towed away. The question is whether making the submarine itself move over land justified the extra machinery and stability problems.

evidence.note: The tracked torpedo craft, its reported tendency to fall over, and the tentatively recalled purpose of using ramps and moving between waterways or maintenance sites.
A detachable wheeled carriage and towing vehicle proposed as a simpler alternative to self-propulsion ashore.

segments.summary: A tracked German midget submarine raises a practical question about whether self-propelled movement ashore justified the complexity compared with a towable carriage.
segments.question: Why did the German midget submarine have tracks, and were they intended for climbing over reefs?
segments.answerShort: The tentatively recalled purpose was to use launch ramps, reach maintenance buildings, and move between waterways over land.

segments.title: Rocket-assisted Tallboy as an answer to giant battleships
segments.body: A rocket-assisted Tallboy is jokingly offered as an RAF answer to the enormous battleships under construction in the game. The underlying proposal pairs a five-ton Tallboy with eight RP-3 rockets, arranged in twos between its fins. In the reading of the project documents offered here, the extra impact speed was intended to improve penetration of bunkers. The rockets would accelerate an existing heavy bomb instead of requiring a wholly new weapon. The idea is placed among postwar British experiments that added rocket assistance to established weapons.

evidence.note: A joking RAF counter to the game battleships leads to the proposed five-ton Tallboy with eight RP-3 rockets.
The project documents are recalled as implying improved bunker penetration through greater impact speed, alongside other postwar rocket-assisted experiments.

segments.summary: The rocket-assisted Tallboy proposal adds eight RP-3 rockets to a heavy bomb to increase impact speed and penetration.

segments.title: T12 Cloudmaker and the limits of giant bomb carriage
segments.body: The T12 Cloudmaker is recalled as a roughly 43,000-pound bomb, approximately twice the size of Grand Slam, intended for the B-36. A modified B-29 served as the test aircraft, with a wing-root mounting recalled for the weapon. Surviving empty casings in the United States are also mentioned. A separate recollection concerns planning for the invasion of Japan, when the US Army Air Forces investigated carrying two Grand Slams on a B-29 for bunker attacks. A photograph is described with one bomb under each wing. These examples concern modified aircraft and proposed or experimental loads.

evidence.note: The recalled 43,000-pound T12, intended B-36 carriage, modified B-29 test mounting, and surviving empty casings.
Recalled investigation and a photograph of a B-29 carrying one Grand Slam under each wing for possible bunker attacks during invasion-of-Japan planning.

segments.summary: The T12 Cloudmaker and a two-Grand-Slam B-29 configuration illustrate the modifications associated with exceptionally large bunker-busting bombs.

segments.title: Why bomber volume can matter more than lifting power
segments.body: The estimate is three Grand Slam-size bombs for a B-52 and one or perhaps two for a B-2. Physical room is the main constraint. The suggested B-52 arrangement places one weapon under each wing root and another in the bomb bay. The B-2's bay dimensions make even two weapons uncertain, with diagonal carriage suggested as a possibility. These are hypothetical arrangements based on space, without a demonstrated installation. A later comparison with the small A-4 Skyhawk reinforces the distinction between an aircraft's size and the weight of weapons it can carry.

evidence.note: Rough Grand Slam carriage estimates, proposed B-52 positions, and uncertainty over fitting one or two bombs in a B-2.
Aircraft space distinguished from lifting capacity, with the A-4 Skyhawk as an example of substantial payload relative to aircraft size.

segments.summary: Hypothetical Grand Slam loads for the B-52 and B-2 depend on room at external stations and inside the bomb bay.
segments.question: How many Grand Slam-size bombs could a B-52 or B-2 carry?
segments.answerShort: Perhaps three for a B-52 and one or two for a B-2, as a rough estimate based mainly on physical space.

segments.title: A Boeing 747 with rotary cruise-missile launchers
segments.body: A suggestion to turn Boeing 747s into bombers prompts recollection of a cruise-missile carrier proposal. The passenger fittings would be removed to make space for four twelve-shot rotary launchers inside the fuselage. That arrangement would use the airliner's large internal volume to carry a substantial missile load. Its practicality is questioned even as the missile-carrying concept is acknowledged.

evidence.note: The recalled 747 cruise-missile carrier proposal with four twelve-shot rotary launchers and doubts about its practicality.

segments.summary: A recalled proposal would replace a 747's passenger accommodation with four twelve-shot rotary cruise-missile launchers.

segments.title: From Vulcan B3 studies to a Concorde bomber
segments.body: A recalled Vulcan B3 proposal would use the Olympus engines associated with Concorde in newly built bombers. The suggestion that it could supercruise receives an immediate disagreement, so that performance claim remains disputed. The subsequent Concorde bomber is a counterfactual design using the passenger and cargo spaces for rotating bomb or missile bays inspired by the Buccaneer. Blue Steel and intermediate-range missiles are suggested payloads. The imagined formation would approach at Mach 2 to 2.5, fire a large missile volley, and leave before the defender could respond effectively. The proposed combination of speed and missile carriage is compared with obtaining a B-1A-like capability about a decade earlier.

evidence.note: TSR-2 cancellation, a recalled Vulcan B3 proposal with Concorde-related Olympus engines, and immediate disagreement over the suggested supercruise capability.
The counterfactual Concorde bomber's rotating bays and possible Blue Steel or intermediate-range missile payloads.
The imagined Mach 2 to 2.5 missile attack and comparison with an earlier B-1A-like capability.

segments.summary: A disputed Vulcan B3 performance claim leads into a counterfactual Concorde bomber with rotating missile bays and a fast approach-and-withdrawal concept.

segments.title: Why use 16.5-inch guns on the German super-battleship?
segments.body: The 16.5-inch caliber is linked from memory to German H41 or H42 studies. Twin 18-inch and 20-inch weapons were considered for the game design because German studies also explored larger guns. Their turret models are judged excessively bulky in Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts. The chosen solution enlarges the game's 16-inch gun to 16.5 inches and uses sixteen barrels in quadruple mounts. The caliber has a remembered historical inspiration, while the final turret arrangement responds to the available game models.

evidence.note: The caliber's remembered H41 or H42 connection and the oversized game models that led to quadruple 16.5-inch mounts.

segments.summary: Remembered H-class studies supply the caliber, while bulky game models for larger twin turrets lead to sixteen 16.5-inch guns in quadruple mounts.
segments.question: Why does the German 90,000-ton design use 16.5-inch guns in quadruple turrets?
segments.answerShort: The caliber is linked to remembered H-class studies, while the game model's oversized twin 18-inch and 20-inch mounts drive the quadruple 16.5-inch layout.

segments.title: An Austro-Hungarian wing-turret challenge
segments.body: The 1920-1925 game challenge requires at least two wing turrets with the same gun caliber as the centerline battery. A 35,000-ton limit is adopted after the initial brief leaves displacement unrestricted. Drachinifel chooses twin 14-inch mounts instead of offset triples, with no cross-deck firing capability. Clarke uses 15-inch guns and a heavy 8-inch secondary battery, including a triple mount superfiring over an after twin 15-inch turret. The secondary battery has a specific purpose in his scenario: an Austro-Hungarian battleship would need to fight past Italian cruisers near the Strait of Otranto. That explanation assumes Austria-Hungary survives into the 1920s because the First World War has not occurred.

evidence.note: The 1920-1925 brief requires same-caliber wing and centerline guns, allows cross-deck fire, and acquires a 35,000-ton limit.
The competing 14-inch and 15-inch layouts, the 8-inch secondary battery, and the hypothetical need to fight Italian cruisers near Otranto.

segments.summary: A 1920s design challenge forces same-caliber wing and centerline turrets into an Austro-Hungarian capital ship.

segments.title: Which US Navy battleships are the historians' favorites?
segments.body: Drachinifel chooses the New Mexico class as his favorite American battleship and includes it among his three favorite battleship designs overall. Clarke prefers the as-built South Dakota class. He also finds the unbuilt 1920s South Dakota design interesting, although it is not the version he selects as his favorite. These are personal preferences, with no comparative technical case offered for either choice.

evidence.note: Personal preferences for New Mexico and the as-built South Dakota class, with a separate qualification about the unbuilt 1920s design.

segments.summary: The New Mexico and as-built South Dakota classes receive the two votes, with additional interest in the unbuilt 1920s South Dakota design.
segments.question: What are Drachinifel's and Dr. Clarke's favorite US Navy dreadnoughts or battleships?
segments.answerShort: Drachinifel chooses the New Mexico class; Dr. Clarke chooses the as-built South Dakota class, while also appreciating the 1920s design.

segments.title: What would an R-class version of HMS Vanguard look like?
segments.body: An R-class-style Vanguard is interpreted as a smaller, cheaper ship analogous to the relationship between the Revenge and Queen Elizabeth classes. The question's intended meaning remains uncertain, and a simplified King George V using four twin turrets is also considered. The preferred Vanguard variant retains the 15-inch battery, potentially using turrets from the old R class. Ten twin 4.5-inch mounts replace the eight twin 5.25-inch mounts, while the smaller hull reduces speed to about 28 knots. This is proposed as a mobilization variant; its wartime performance is not worked through in detail.

evidence.note: The question is interpreted as a smaller and cheaper Vanguard analogous to the relationship between the Revenge and Queen Elizabeth classes.
The proposed mobilization variant keeps 15-inch guns, substitutes ten twin 4.5-inch mounts, and reduces speed to 28 knots.

segments.summary: A proposed mobilization Vanguard keeps the 15-inch battery while reducing hull size and speed and changing the secondary armament.
segments.question: How might an R-class-style, more economical variant of HMS Vanguard have measured up during the Second World War?
segments.answerShort: As a smaller mobilization Vanguard retaining the 15-inch battery, with ten twin 4.5-inch mounts and roughly 28 knots instead of the full ship's higher speed and complexity.

segments.title: Alternative designs for HMS Agincourt
segments.body: The challenge recreates alternatives for the unbuilt sixth Queen Elizabeth, allowing small-tube boilers and heavier guns to arrive early. Drachinifel fits nine 15-inch/42 guns in triple turrets and a 13-inch inclined belt. Clarke chooses six 18-inch/45 guns, 28 knots, and a 16-inch belt, with triple 4-inch mounts and casemate 6-inch guns. The heavier-gun design promises greater range and more damage from each shell. Its six-gun battery offers fewer shells for spotting and target acquisition than the nine-gun alternative. Both ships are game reconstructions of competing interpretations, and the game's technology dates require adjustment to make the chosen guns available.

evidence.note: The unbuilt Queen Elizabeth challenge, preferences for triple 15-inch or twin 18-inch turrets, and the game's inconsistent gun availability.
The completed designs' batteries, armor, speed, and the tradeoff between salvo volume, target acquisition, range, and individual shell effect.

segments.summary: Competing Agincourt alternatives explore triple 15-inch guns and twin 18-inch guns under counterfactual British technology assumptions.

segments.title: What should a Type 83 destroyer class be called?
segments.body: Duke of Edinburgh is the preferred class name in this hypothetical naming exercise. The attraction is the pairing of HMS Queen Elizabeth with an escort named Duke of Edinburgh. Princess Royal is also proposed for an individual ship. These are personal naming suggestions, conditional on the Royal Navy adopting the proposed Type 83 concept.

evidence.note: The hypothetical Duke of Edinburgh class name, its pairing with Queen Elizabeth, and the proposed individual name Princess Royal.

segments.summary: Duke of Edinburgh is proposed as a Type 83 class name, with Princess Royal suggested for an individual ship.
segments.question: If the Royal Navy adopted the proposed Type 83 concept, what should the class be called?
segments.answerShort: Duke of Edinburgh class, with Princess Royal among the possible ship names.

segments.title: Could a Swedish coastal-defence battleship challenge Hoche?
segments.body: A Swedish coastal-defence battleship of Hoche's era is accepted as having a chance against her. A later claim that Hoche would defeat Sweden's most advanced warships around 1890 meets disagreement. One participant declines a firm comparison because he does not know the composition of the Swedish fleet at that date. No Swedish class is identified, so the matchup remains general and qualified.

evidence.note: The question about a same-era Swedish coastal-defence battleship and the affirmative response.
The disputed claim about Sweden's leading ships in 1890 and the stated limit of one participant's fleet knowledge.

segments.summary: A Swedish coastal-defence battleship is considered a plausible challenger, but the fleet-specific comparison remains unresolved.
segments.question: Could a Swedish coastal-defence battleship of the same era have a chance against Hoche?
segments.answerShort: Yes, but no Swedish class is identified and the later claim that Hoche could defeat Sweden's leading ships remains disputed.

segments.title: Does the Venator count as a true carrier?
segments.body: The Venator qualifies as a carrier under a definition that allows substantial direct combat armament alongside aviation. Calling it a battlecarrier recognizes those combined roles. Requiring a carrier to serve only aviation would exclude many Star Wars capital ships because single-purpose designs are rare in the setting. The Imperial Star Destroyer is placed farther toward the mainline gun-capital-ship role. These classifications concern fictional vessels and depend on how narrowly each naval type is defined.

evidence.note: The distinction between a single-purpose carrier, the Venator as a battlecarrier, and the Imperial Star Destroyer as a mainline gun capital ship.

segments.summary: The Venator is classified as a battlecarrier because it combines a major embarked air group with capital-ship armament.
segments.question: Does the Venator-class Star Destroyer count as an actual carrier?
segments.answerShort: Yes, as a battlecarrier: it combines carrier aviation with capital-ship gun power rather than serving as a single-purpose flight-deck ship.

segments.title: Do Battlestars qualify as battlecarriers?
segments.body: There is disagreement over whether Battlestars qualify as battlecarriers. One view accepts the label, while the other focuses on Galactica's lack of a distinct main gun battery. She has guns and can launch nuclear missiles, but the stricter classification calls her a heavily armed carrier. Lexington-class aircraft carriers before the removal of their 8-inch guns provide the real naval comparison. The disagreement concerns the significance of the ship's primary armament.

evidence.note: Opposing classifications of Galactica and the comparison with Lexington-class carriers carrying 8-inch guns.

segments.summary: Galactica's lack of a distinct main gun battery prompts disagreement over whether she is a battlecarrier or a heavily armed carrier.
segments.question: Do Battlestars such as Galactica count as battlecarriers?
segments.answerShort: Opinions differ: one view accepts the battlecarrier label, while the stricter view calls Galactica a heavily armed carrier because she lacks a distinct main gun battery.

segments.title: How thick could British foundries forge battleship armor?
segments.body: British foundries are credited with the ability to forge battleship belt plate about 16 inches thick in the period of the Agincourt design exercise. The figure is described as approximately the same limit as turret armor. It provides an industrial basis for the reconstructed ship's 16-inch belt, without a further distinction between armor grades or manufacturing processes.

evidence.note: An approximate 16-inch British manufacturing limit for belt plate, compared with turret armor.

segments.summary: British belt-plate manufacture is credited with an approximate 16-inch limit for the period of the Agincourt design exercise.
segments.question: What was the maximum thickness British foundries could forge for battleship belt armor in this era?
segments.answerShort: About 16 inches, comparable to the maximum thickness used for turret armor.

segments.title: Why consider 18-inch guns for the unbuilt Agincourt?
segments.body: Clarke favors twin 18-inch turrets for Agincourt as an inference from British gun development and the ship's cancellation. He argues that the 18-inch guns later used on Furious originated in a battleship requirement, and treats the unbuilt sixth Queen Elizabeth as the likely intended recipient. The stated technological reason for cancellation is another part of that interpretation, especially because the yard had already built Queen Elizabeth. Enlarging a twin turret also appears a plausible development path from earlier British heavy guns. British industry already had experience with triple turrets for export, however, so triple 15-inch mounts remained within its capabilities. Later K2 and M2 studies provide examples of twin-18-inch arrangements, but drawing a design does not prove an intention to build it.

evidence.note: Clarke's inference linking 18-inch gun development and Agincourt's technological cancellation, alongside the alternative case for triple turrets.
K2 and M2 twin-18-inch studies and the qualification that alternatives could be drawn to explain why another layout was preferred.

segments.summary: A proposed connection between British 18-inch gun development and Agincourt's cancellation supports one interpretation of her intended armament.

segments.title: Why an archived warship design may never have been intended for construction
segments.body: An archived design can document an alternative investigated to establish why it should be rejected. Proposed American-gun refits of the Nelson class illustrate the danger of treating every surviving drawing as a construction intention. More than two dozen Nelson refit options are described for 1941-1944, varying the numbers and arrangements of 5.25-inch, 6-inch, 4.5-inch, 5-inch/38, and 5-inch/54 guns. Comparing those alternatives helped identify an affordable increase in fighting effectiveness. It also equipped naval staff to explain to politicians and the Treasury why an apparently attractive proposal was impractical.

evidence.note: Designs used to justify rejecting alternatives and the risk of interpreting Nelson American-gun refit drawings without their institutional context.
More than two dozen 1941-1944 Nelson refit options, their alternative gun batteries, and the search for cost-effective improvements.

segments.summary: Nelson's many proposed refits tested affordability and supported arguments against proposals as well as preparing ships for construction.

segments.title: What is the largest warship Hoche could defeat?
segments.body: Hoche's guns and armor are judged sufficient against the previous generation of central-battery and barbette ironclads. A higher rate of fire could also give her a chance against Inflexible and large contemporary Italian ironclads. Her underwater torpedoes create a disputed possibility of defeating much larger opponents at the short battle ranges expected in this period. One view stresses the damage a successful hit could inflict; the objection is that early Whitehead torpedoes could fail on entering the water, miss, or fail to function after striking. Poor gunnery accuracy also limits confidence, although ships could fire many more shells than torpedoes. Hoche's large 3.9-inch battery offers another source of firepower, provided the target is within range and firing arc. A possible lucky torpedo hit therefore does not establish a dependable advantage over a particular larger warship.

evidence.note: Earlier ironclads as plausible opponents and the claimed potential of underwater torpedoes at short battle ranges.
Disagreement over early Whitehead reliability, the greater number of shells available, and the range and arc limits of Hoche's 3.9-inch battery.

segments.summary: Hoche is credited with plausible gun-and-armor advantages over earlier ironclads, while unreliable torpedoes complicate claims about defeating larger ships.
segments.question: What is the largest technologically contemporary ship Hoche could take on and defeat?
segments.answerShort: Earlier central-battery and barbette ironclads are credible opponents; early Whitehead torpedoes create only a remote chance against much larger ships.

segments.title: A deliberately weak Manchurian battleship
segments.body: The hypothetical customer is Japan's Chinese client state in 1940, interpreted as Manchukuo. A Japanese yard must build it an impressive-looking battleship using technology from 1920-1940 while ensuring the result cannot threaten Japan. Maintenance at Port Arthur is another constraint. The designers distinguish a ship that is ineffective from one that Japanese planners would merely consider inferior, because those approaches can produce different results. The strict interpretation requires fundamental flaws that would let a Japanese heavy cruiser inflict serious damage. The design brief consequently combines the customer's desire for prestige with the supplier's determination to retain military control.

evidence.note: The hypothetical Japanese-built Manchukuo battleship, its technology period, Port Arthur support constraint, and the distinction between actual weakness and perceived inferiority.
The strict requirement for a fundamentally flawed battleship that a Japanese heavy cruiser could seriously damage.

segments.summary: A 1940 Japanese yard must build a prestigious-looking battleship for a Chinese client state without creating a threat to Japan.

segments.title: Would coal suit a Manchurian battleship?
segments.body: Coal firing is recommended for the hypothetical Manchurian battleship because Manchuria has substantial coal seams. That makes the fuel choice defensible in the client's own circumstances. It also complicates the challenge to design a bad battleship: a feature that looks inferior to Japanese planners can still be useful to the recipient. Local fuel availability changes how the same propulsion choice is judged.

evidence.note: The recommendation for coal firing, Manchuria's coal deposits, and the distinction between suitability for the client and Japanese perceptions.

segments.summary: Manchuria's coal deposits make coal firing a practical choice despite its inferior appearance to Japanese planners.
segments.question: Could the hypothetical Manchurian battleship be coal-fired?
segments.answerShort: Yes, and coal is recommended because Manchuria has substantial local deposits.

segments.title: An impressive battleship designed to be unmanageable
segments.body: Drachinifel's client-state proposal advertises 18.1-inch guns, 29 knots, long range, modern armor, and a large oxygen-torpedo battery. The apparent strength conceals a deliberate maintenance trap in the game challenge. At almost 55,000 tons, the ship has only a 14-inch belt and 5-inch deck, protection compared with that of a 35,000-ton battleship. Very long gun barrels, heavy electrically driven turrets, underwater oxygen-torpedo tubes, a single bottom, and minimal underwater protection supply the intended weaknesses. Diesel propulsion and extensive electrical machinery are chosen as burdens on the recipient's support system, while five large ammunition types complicate supply. A suggestion that Japan might seize and repair the ship meets the objection that the accumulated faults would leave it shuttling between repair facilities.

evidence.note: Advertised performance and deliberately adverse choices in armament, machinery, fuel, and underwater protection.
Disagreement about salvaging the design and the burden of five large ammunition types.

segments.summary: A deliberately unreliable game design combines an intimidating battery with machinery, protection, and supply demands intended to overwhelm its recipient.

segments.title: A 35,000-ton ship Japan might underestimate
segments.body: Clarke takes a different approach to the client-state brief: a ship that Japanese planners would consider weak could still serve Manchurian needs. His game design has nine 14-inch guns, twin 4-inch dual-purpose weapons, coal firing, and a speed of 28 knots within 35,000 tons. In this imagined procurement decision, Japan dismisses the smaller guns and modest specification without recognizing the recipient's practical gains. Reduced beam and draft improve access to ports; possible canal use is suggested rather than established. The original thought of 24 knots gives way to 28 because a slow battleship would be difficult to sell by 1940.

evidence.note: Clarke's nine-gun, 28-knot design and his argument about Japanese perceptions, port access, and saleability.

segments.summary: A modest coal-fired design could look inferior to Japan while offering Manchukuo usable firepower and easier port access.

segments.title: Designing for Chinese cruisers and local maintenance
segments.body: Fleet judges his proposed battleship against the Republican Chinese cruisers it would actually be expected to fight. It has a ten-gun broadside of short 12-inch/30 weapons, 8-inch casemates, a 4-inch dual-purpose battery, and a speed of 24 knots. That leaves it vulnerable to foreign capital ships, but would let it outrun and outgun the approximately 23-knot coal-fired cruisers used as its regional comparison. Coal firing and minimal beam and draft suit the intended user's support constraints. The game forces turbine propulsion, although Fleet would prefer forced-lubrication triple-expansion engines because components could be removed and repaired more readily. He also sees the short main guns as useful for high-angle shelling, making the design a proposed regional flagship rather than a competitor for first-line foreign battleships.

evidence.note: Fleet's armament and speed, Republican Chinese cruiser comparison, and preferred triple-expansion machinery unavailable in the game.

segments.summary: A 24-knot game design trades international competitiveness for firepower, port access, and machinery suited to its intended regional opponent.

segments.title: A client battleship still needs somewhere to dock
segments.body: The Manchurian design judgment turns on competing interpretations of the brief. One judge favors Clarke's proposal because the recipient could reasonably receive and dock it. Drachinifel's deliberately unreliable ship raises the more basic objection that its size would leave nowhere suitable to put it. Another judge gives priority to making the battleship genuinely bad and favors the design expected to spend most of its time alongside. The prompt's author gives Fleet the deciding vote. Port compatibility and the requirement for poor performance produce different winners among the judges.

evidence.note: Contrasting verdicts based on dock access and the requirement for a battleship that performs badly.

segments.summary: The judges disagree over whether port access or deliberate unreliability should decide the client-state challenge.

segments.title: An early-1930s USS Constitution battlecruiser
segments.body: The final Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts challenge calls for a US Navy battlecruiser of 30,000-33,000 tons, with 1932 chosen as the design year. Its performance must justify the name Constitution. The available game hulls constrain the project: a large-cruiser hull is needed to reach the requested displacement, and it limits the main battery to 15-inch guns. A 14-inch battery offers room for the desired speed within that size. The designers also invoke the run-up to the Second London Naval Treaty when explaining their caliber choice.

evidence.note: A US battlecruiser brief of 30,000-33,000 tons, with 1932 selected as its year.
Game hull limits, a 15-inch ceiling, and the choice of 14-inch guns to accommodate speed.

segments.summary: A 1932 game-design brief combines the Constitution name with a 30,000-33,000-ton limit and a fast capital-ship role.

segments.title: USS Indiana as America's first battleship effort
segments.body: USS Indiana had serious flaws, including unbalanced 13-inch guns that increased the ship's list when trained to port or starboard. Even so, the US Navy had moved from Civil War-era monitors through Maine and Texas to Indiana in roughly a decade. Indiana rates as a good first effort within that rapid transition. A comparison with navies that already had mature battleship design systems produces a less favorable judgment, because those rivals began with much more experience.

evidence.note: Indiana's gun-balance flaw and the distinction between a first effort and mature foreign battleship designs.

segments.summary: USS Indiana is judged a strong first step for a navy rapidly moving beyond Civil War-era monitors.
segments.question: How should USS Indiana BB-1 be rated as a first American battleship effort?
segments.answerShort: A good first effort despite important flaws, especially when measured against the US Navy's rapid transition from monitors rather than mature foreign designs.

segments.title: Jet aircraft on straight-deck carriers
segments.body: Straight-deck carriers operated jet aircraft before angled flight decks became standard. Angled decks addressed problems associated with higher landing speeds and the way carriers organized launches and recoveries. Those changes also affected sortie rate. During the Korean War, straight-deck carriers operated jets or piston aircraft according to their air groups, without needing an angled deck to make flight operations possible.

evidence.note: Straight-deck jet operations in the Korean War and the landing-speed and sortie-rate problems addressed by angled decks.

segments.summary: Straight flight decks could operate jets, while angled decks mainly improved landing safety and sortie flow.
segments.question: Did the US Navy have difficulty operating jet aircraft from straight-deck carriers?
segments.answerShort: Not fundamentally; straight decks operated jets successfully, while angled decks solved landing-speed, safety, and sortie-rate problems.

segments.title: Was the development of modern naval warfare set in stone?
segments.body: Modern naval warfare could have developed differently if wars, treaties, and carrier programs had occurred on different schedules. In a counterfactual treaty system beginning in 1930, Britain could already have built G3 and N3 capital ships and moved on to a further generation. Germany would then have to decide whether its historical route back to battleship construction still made sense. Scharnhorst's 11-inch armament is explained here in terms of the guns Germany could supply at the time, a constraint that would matter more against such powerful rivals. Carrier conversions of unfinished Admiral-class hulls introduce another difficulty: prolonged exposure on the building ways could affect the ships' condition. Changes in capital-ship protection and carrier development would in turn alter the problems faced by aircraft designers.

evidence.note: Counterfactual treaty timing, G3 and N3 construction, German gun availability, and the condition of unfinished carrier-conversion hulls.

segments.summary: Later naval treaties and another generation of battleships would change German rearmament, carrier conversions, and the demands on naval aircraft.
segments.question: Was the development of modern naval warfare mostly set in stone, or could it have evolved differently?
segments.answerShort: It was highly contingent; different wars, treaty timing, capital-ship programs, and carrier development could have produced very different fleets and doctrine.

segments.title: Reading history through the choices available at the time
segments.body: Knowing the eventual outcome can distort the way earlier decisions are interpreted. Reading history forward means reconstructing the options available to people at the time and asking why some were taken while others were closed off. Starting with a predetermined explanation risks collecting confirmation for it instead of investigating the causes. Alternate-history questions offer a way to examine those choices.

evidence.note: Forward reading of history, unrealized branches, and the risk of seeking confirmation for a known outcome.

segments.summary: Historical explanation requires attention to unrealized options and contemporary constraints, as well as the path events ultimately took.

segments.title: A fast Tennessee with space for a flagship staff
segments.body: Drachinifel's game-built Constitution combines twelve 14-inch/50 guns in four triple turrets with 33 knots at just under 33,000 tons. He links the guns to the Tennessee class and invokes contemporary interest in 14-inch armament when explaining the choice. The Old Ironsides name also drives maximum available underwater protection, reinforced bulkheads, and flood-control equipment. A 13.5-inch belt and 6-inch deck accompany 12-inch turret protection, with little displacement remaining. Radar is excluded for the early-1930s setting. Removing a pair of twin 5-inch/38 mounts provides extra flag-officer space, using USS South Dakota as the accommodation analogy.

evidence.note: Drachinifel's battery, speed, protection settings, early-1930s electronics, and flagship-space tradeoff.

segments.summary: A game design combines Tennessee-type main guns and 33 knots, then sacrifices some secondary armament for flagship accommodation.

segments.title: Extra protection and disputed antiaircraft equipment
segments.body: Clarke's competing Constellation game design also carries twelve 14-inch/50 guns and makes 33 knots. Its reported displacement is 32,797 tons and its range is 21,000 kilometers, with deep draft used in the design. A 14-inch belt is slightly thicker than its rival's, while a less advanced citadel setting is selected as more appropriate to the period. The heavy antiaircraft outfit prompts a chronology caveat: one designer pulls back from extensive 40 mm armament because the scenario is set in the early 1930s. The proposed use of 1.1-inch weapons as a substitute makes clear that the displayed game fit and the intended historical equipment need separate consideration.

evidence.note: Clarke's displacement, range, belt and citadel choice, followed by the early-1930s antiaircraft-fit caveat.

segments.summary: Two similar game battlecruisers differ in protection and antiaircraft fit, with period suitability raised during their comparison.

segments.title: A conservative Constitution built from mature weapons
segments.body: Fleet's game proposal favors an eight-gun 14-inch/50 battery in four twin turrets and weapons he considers suitable for getting an early-1930s ship built quickly. He selects single 5-inch/38 mounts because the twin version has yet to go to sea in the chronology he is using. Game models stand in for the intended 1.1-inch Chicago Piano installations where the desired mount cannot be fitted. The design matches its competitors' 33-knot speed and range, but lacks their super-heavy shells and carries only a 12-inch belt and 3-inch deck. During review, automatic loading and radar are identified as inappropriate settings for the proposed 1932 ship. The judges prefer the twelve-gun alternatives for combat power, while acknowledging the conservative design's approach to weapon availability.

evidence.note: Fleet's eight-gun proposal, intended 1.1-inch mounts, single 5-inch/38 rationale, and corrections to automatic-loading and radar settings.
Comparison of displacement headroom, flagship accommodation, main-gun numbers, and armor.

segments.summary: A third entrant trades twelve-gun firepower for an eight-gun battery and existing single 5-inch/38 mounts that could reach service with less development risk.

segments.title: Choosing between flagship space and extra armor
segments.body: The two twelve-gun Constitution proposals leave the judges with a close choice. Clarke's design has more displacement available for later additions and carries a 14-inch belt and approximately 7-inch deck, compared with Drachinifel's 13.5-inch belt and 6-inch deck. Both include flag facilities, but Drachinifel's are roomier. Constitution's historical presence missions provide the reason for one verdict favoring the extra accommodation. Another interpretation of the Old Ironsides name favors the heavier armor, while Fleet's eight-gun proposal loses ground through its smaller battery and lighter protection.

evidence.note: Displacement margin, flagship accommodation, stated armor differences, and competing interpretations of the Constitution name.

segments.summary: Similar twelve-gun battlecruisers offer a choice between extra armor and growth margin or roomier flagship accommodation.
